div.div:
The Fencing Token Defense:
• Problem: A delayed message with an old state payload arrives out of order after a newer update committed.
• Condition: v_fencing > v_current
• Stale Packet Action: If token ≤ current, message is dropped without mutating state.
• Guarantee: Protects against Byzantine network reordering.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 1268px; height: 1px; padding-top: 459px; margin-left: 30px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #000000; background-color: #FFFFFF;

display: inline-block; font-size: 10px; font-family: 'Comic Sans MS'; color: light-dark(#000000, #ededed); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; background-color: light-dark(#FFFFFF, #121212); white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div:
Deduplication Table Sizing & Eviction Invariants:
• Sliding Time Window: Deduplication tables must retain message IDs only for the maximum expected redelivery window (e.g., 7 days). Retaining IDs indefinitely creates table bloat that degrades index lookup performance.
• Partition Partitioning: In high-throughput systems (>50,000 msgs/sec), partition the deduplication table by hash(message_id) or date range to maintain b-tree indexes entirely within RAM.
• Atomic Scope: Deduplication token check and business logic state mutation must share the exact same database transaction. Checking dedup in Redis and updating PostgreSQL in separate calls re-introduces the dual-write race.
